claims.text: Engineered interfaces in multilayer HEA coatings block and slow dislocation motion and climb.
Interface-mediated dislocation blockage reduces creep relative to a similar monolithic HEA coating.
Controlled deposition by methods such as magnetron sputtering or laser cladding can produce well-defined alternating HEA layers with high lattice distortion.
Deposition parameters such as bias voltage and layer thickness can be used to create distinct, coherent interfaces.
A monolithic HEA coating processed under otherwise identical conditions is an appropriate baseline for isolating the effect of periodic interfaces.
Nanoindentation can be used to characterize time-dependent deformation in HEAs at small length scales.
Nanoindentation creep results are directly representative of coating behavior under the stated service regimes.
Lattice mismatch and intrinsic lattice distortion cause multilayer interfaces to impede dislocation motion and prevent dislocation climb.
HEAs can exhibit a transition from diffusion-controlled creep at low stress to dislocation-dominated creep at higher stress.
Applied stress at elevated temperature generates dislocations in the HEA layers.
Multilayer interfaces force dislocations to pile up or change paths.
Obstructing dislocation glide and climb at interfaces increases the effective activation energy for creep.
Dislocations move more freely in a monolithic HEA coating than in the corresponding multilayer coating.
Under identical test conditions, the multilayer coating will have lower creep strain or creep rate than the monolithic coating.
The proposed interface mechanism is most applicable in stress and temperature regimes where creep is dislocation-mediated.
Diffusion is typically sufficiently slow in HEAs for the proposed interface mechanism to dominate.
The mechanism may become less significant when layer thickness is outside an optimal range.
The quantitative contributions of lattice distortion and slow diffusion to creep resistance are unresolved.
Dislocation pile-ups or blockage at multilayer interfaces should be observable by post-test microscopy.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant creep reduction, or failure to observe interfacial dislocation blockage, would falsify the hypothesis.
